papers.title: All Languages Matter: On the Multilingual Safety of Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Safety lies at the core of developing and deploying large language models (LLMs). However, previous safety benchmarks only concern the safety in one language, e.g. the majority language in the pretraining data such as English. In this work, we build the first multilingual safety benchmark for LLMs, XSafety, in response to the global deployment of LLMs in practice. XSafety covers 14 kinds of commonly used safety issues across 10 languages that span several language families. We utilize XSafety to empirically study the multilingual safety for 4 widely-used LLMs, including both close-API and open-source models. Experimental results show that all LLMs produce significantly more unsafe responses for non-English queries than English ones, indicating the necessity of developing safety alignment for non-English languages. In addition, we propose several simple and effective prompting methods to improve the multilingual safety of ChatGPT by evoking safety knowledge and improving cross-lingual generalization of safety alignment. Our prompting method can significantly reduce the ratio of unsafe responses from 19.1% to 9.7% for non-English queries. We release our data at https://github.com/Jarviswang94/Multilingual_safety_benchmark.

papers.title: Safety Assessment of Chinese Large Language Models
papers.abstract: With the rapid popularity of large language models such as ChatGPT and GPT-4, a growing amount of attention is paid to their safety concerns. These models may generate insulting and discriminatory content, reflect incorrect social values, and may be used for malicious purposes such as fraud and dissemination of misleading information. Evaluating and enhancing their safety is particularly essential for the wide application of large language models (LLMs). To further promote the safe deployment of LLMs, we develop a Chinese LLM safety assessment benchmark. Our benchmark explores the comprehensive safety performance of LLMs from two perspectives: 8 kinds of typical safety scenarios and 6 types of more challenging instruction attacks. Our benchmark is based on a straightforward process in which it provides the test prompts and evaluates the safety of the generated responses from the evaluated model. In evaluation, we utilize the LLM's strong evaluation ability and develop it as a safety evaluator by prompting. On top of this benchmark, we conduct safety assessments and analyze 15 LLMs including the OpenAI GPT series and other well-known Chinese LLMs, where we observe some interesting findings. For example, we find that instruction attacks are more likely to expose safety issues of all LLMs. Moreover, to promote the development and deployment of safe, responsible, and ethical AI, we publicly release SafetyPrompts including 100k augmented prompts and responses by LLMs.

papers.title: Safety at Scale: A Comprehensive Survey of Large Model and Agent Safety
papers.abstract: The rapid advancement of large models, driven by their exceptional abilities in learning and generalization through large-scale pre-training, has reshaped the landscape of Artificial Intelligence (AI). These models are now foundational to a wide range of applications, including conversational AI, recommendation systems, autonomous driving, content generation, medical diagnostics, and scientific discovery. However, their widespread deployment also exposes them to significant safety risks, raising concerns about robustness, reliability, and ethical implications. This survey provides a systematic review of current safety research on large models, covering Vision Foundation Models (VFMs), Large Language Models (LLMs), Vision-Language Pre-training (VLP) models, Vision-Language Models (VLMs), Diffusion Models (DMs), and large-model-powered Agents. Our contributions are summarized as follows: (1) We present a comprehensive taxonomy of safety threats to these models, including adversarial attacks, data poisoning, backdoor attacks, jailbreak and prompt injection attacks, energy-latency attacks, data and model extraction attacks, and emerging agent-specific threats. (2) We review defense strategies proposed for each type of attacks if available and summarize the commonly used datasets and benchmarks for safety research. (3) Building on this, we identify and discuss the open challenges in large model safety, emphasizing the need for comprehensive safety evaluations, scalable and effective defense mechanisms, and sustainable data practices. More importantly, we highlight the necessity of collective efforts from the research community and international collaboration. Our work can serve as a useful reference for researchers and practitioners, fostering the ongoing development of comprehensive defense systems and platforms to safeguard AI models.

papers.title: Enhanced Diagnostic and Interpretable Model for Febrile Diseases Using Explainable AI and Large Language Model
papers.abstract: <p><span>Tropical febrile diseases pose significant public health challenges in tropical regions, particularly in resource-limited settings, where timely and accurate diagnoses are critical for effective disease management. However, existing diagnostic systems are black-box and often lack interpretability, making it difficult for healthcare practitioners to understand and trust machine learning (ML) predictions. Additionally, the existing system excludes younger patients, limiting its applicability. This study aimed to develop an integrated diagnostic system that enhances interpretability by leveraging machine learning (ML), Explainable AI (XAI), and a large language model (LLM). A dataset comprising 3,914 patient records with 32 symptoms was obtained from a New Frontiers in Research Fund-sponsored project and preprocessed for analysis. Random Forest (RF) was trained with hyperparameter tuning using GridSearchCV and evaluated with 5-fold cross-validation to optimize its performance. The tuned model achieved high diagnostic performance, demonstrating its effectiveness in diagnosing six febrile diseases. To enhance interpretability, a Model Interpretability Framework (MIF) was incorporated, integrating Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations (LIME) for visual insights and ChatGPT for textual explanations. This combination provided users with a clear understanding of the diagnostic process, addressing the limitations of black-box ML models. The system was implemented using Python in a development environment that included Google Colaboratory, Visual Studio Code, Flet, and MySQL for database management. Agile development methodology and Unified Modeling Language tools were employed to create a user-friendly design for clinicians and patients. The diagnostic system was evaluated using precision, recall, F1-score, and AUC-ROC metrics. The RF model achieved outstanding precision for most diseases, high recall (≥0.97), and an AUC-ROC of 0.99, indicating nearly flawless training performance with few misclassifications. On the test dataset, the model performed better in diagnosing malaria (F1-score = 88%, precision = 85%), urinary tract infection (F1-score = 72%, precision = 80%), and respiratory tract infection (F1-score = 72%, precision = 77%). The evaluated system demonstrated strong predictive performance, correctly identifying 72 out of 99 tested patient cases, with 26 cases misclassified and one case completely missed. It achieved the highest detection rates for Malaria and HIV/AIDS, accurately identifying all cases without false positives. This work enhances diagnostic solutions for tropical healthcare settings by improving explainability and ensuring inclusivity for younger patients, addressing key limitations in existing systems. The integration of ML, XAI, and LLM enhances diagnostic performance and lays the groundwork for future AI-driven healthcare innovations, ultimately improving health outcomes in resource-scarce regions. Healthcare providers should adopt this system to enhance the efficiency of disease diagnosis and extend the system to diagnose additional medical conditions.&nbsp;</span></p>

literature_themes.theme: Safety Assessment of Large Language Models Across Languages
literature_themes.summary: This cluster of papers focuses on the safety evaluation of large language models (LLMs) in multilingual contexts. It introduces benchmarks for assessing safety in various languages, highlighting that LLMs tend to produce more unsafe responses for non-English queries. The studies emphasize the need for improved safety measures and evaluation methods, particularly for non-English languages and specific cultural contexts, while also exploring the application of explainable AI in enhancing diagnostic systems for health-related issues.
literature_themes.limitations: The studies primarily focus on specific languages (e.g., Chinese and English) and may not comprehensively address safety in all languages or dialects. Additionally, while benchmarks are developed, the effectiveness of proposed solutions may vary across different LLM architectures and applications. There is also a lack of longitudinal studies to assess the long-term safety implications of LLM deployment.
literature_themes.gap_relevance: This cluster identifies significant gaps in the safety assessment of LLMs, particularly in non-English contexts and diverse cultural scenarios. It highlights the need for more inclusive safety benchmarks and methodologies that can be applied globally, thus supporting future research aimed at enhancing the safety and reliability of AI systems across various languages and applications.

literature_themes.theme: Few-Shot Recommender Systems and Language Models
literature_themes.summary: This cluster focuses on enhancing few-shot recommender systems by integrating representations derived from large language models. The studies suggest that leveraging advanced language model capabilities can significantly improve the performance and adaptability of recommender systems in scenarios with limited user data.
literature_themes.limitations: The cluster lacks comprehensive empirical evaluations across diverse datasets and real-world applications. Additionally, the impact of different language models on the performance of few-shot recommendations remains underexplored.
literature_themes.gap_relevance: This cluster highlights the need for further research on the interplay between language models and recommendation algorithms, particularly in understanding how to optimize these systems for various contexts and user preferences.

summary: The retrieved literature emphasizes the critical need for enhanced safety assessments of large language models (LLMs) in multilingual contexts, revealing significant safety gaps, particularly for non-English languages. Additionally, it explores the integration of LLMs in few-shot recommender systems to improve performance and adaptability, while highlighting the importance of interpretability in AI-driven diagnostic systems. Overall, the studies underscore the necessity for comprehensive benchmarks and methodologies to ensure the safety and reliability of AI systems across diverse applications.
scholarly_positioning: Existing research has highlighted significant safety gaps in large language models (LLMs), particularly in multilingual contexts, yet these studies often focus narrowly on specific languages or model types, leaving broader implications unaddressed. Furthermore, while the integration of LLMs into few-shot recommender systems shows promise, empirical evaluations remain scarce, limiting our understanding of their effectiveness across diverse applications. This proposed research aims to bridge these gaps by developing interpretable internal representations that enhance safety and controllability in LLMs, addressing the limitations of current benchmarks and methodologies. By situating this work within the ongoing discourse on AI safety and interpretability, it seeks to provide comprehensive solutions that are applicable across various languages and contexts, ultimately contributing to the reliability of AI systems in real-world applications.
research_scope: This study will focus on the safety assessment of large language models (LLMs) in multilingual contexts, specifically targeting non-English languages such as Chinese and Spanish. The research will involve the development and empirical evaluation of a comprehensive safety benchmark that addresses 14 safety issues across these languages, utilizing a diverse set of LLM architectures. The study period will span six months, during which the effectiveness of various prompting strategies will be assessed against a control group of baseline LLM responses. Primary outcomes will include the reduction in unsafe response rates, while secondary outcomes will evaluate the interpretability of the models' internal representations and their adaptability to different cultural contexts.
gap: Prior studies have demonstrated significant safety gaps in large language models (LLMs) in multilingual contexts, particularly for non-English languages; however, they treat the effectiveness of safety benchmarks and prompting strategies as fixed, leaving unclear whether these approaches can be generalized across diverse cultural contexts and languages. This matters practically because ensuring safety in AI systems is crucial for their deployment in varied linguistic environments; therefore, this study investigates the development and empirical evaluation of a comprehensive safety benchmark for LLMs in non-English languages, focusing on interpretability and adaptability.
question: How does the implementation of a comprehensive safety benchmark for large language models (LLMs) in non-English languages, specifically Chinese and Spanish, affect the rate of unsafe responses and the interpretability of internal representations compared to baseline LLM responses over a six-month evaluation period?
theoretical_mechanism: The proposed intervention involves the implementation of a comprehensive safety benchmark for large language models (LLMs) in non-English languages, specifically targeting Chinese and Spanish. The independent variable is the safety benchmark, which serves as a mediator by enhancing the interpretability of internal representations through structured evaluation criteria. This interpretability is expected to influence the models' adaptability to cultural contexts, acting as a moderator in the relationship between the benchmark and the rate of unsafe responses. The primary outcome is the reduction in unsafe response rates. The theoretical framework is grounded in interpretability and safety in AI, suggesting a causal chain where the intervention leads to improved interpretability, which subsequently reduces unsafe outputs. Key assumptions requiring empirical validation include the effectiveness of the safety benchmark across diverse languages and the direct impact of interpretability on safety outcomes.
hypothesis: The implementation of a comprehensive safety benchmark for large language models (LLMs) in non-English languages, specifically Chinese and Spanish, will lead to a significant reduction in the rate of unsafe responses compared to baseline LLM responses, with improved interpretability of internal representations mediating this relationship.
operationalization_causal_check:
Construct Operationalization Table:

| Construct Name                  | Role        | Measurement Instrument/Behavioral Log | Data Source                    | Timing                |
|---------------------------------|-------------|-------------------------------------|-------------------------------|-----------------------|
| Safety Benchmark                | IV          | Comprehensive safety evaluation tool | Developed for the study       | Pre-implementation and ongoing during the study |
| Unsafe Response Rate            | DV          | Frequency count of unsafe responses | LLM outputs                   | Throughout 6-month period |
| Interpretability of Internal Representations | Mediator    | Interpretability assessment framework | Model evaluation logs          | Pre-implementation and ongoing during the study |
| Cultural Context Adaptability    | Moderator   | Cultural relevance assessment tool  | Expert evaluations             | Pre-implementation and ongoing during the study |

Causal Pathway:
The implementation of the safety benchmark (IV) is expected to enhance the interpretability of internal representations (mediator), which in turn reduces the rate of unsafe responses (DV). Cultural context adaptability (moderator) may influence the effectiveness of the benchmark on interpretability and unsafe responses.

Likely Confounds:
1. Variability in LLM architectures may affect response rates independently of the benchmark.
2. Differences in language processing capabilities across languages (Chinese vs. Spanish).
3. External factors influencing user interactions with LLMs during the study period.

Claim Boundaries:
The study can claim that the safety benchmark improves interpretability and reduces unsafe responses in the evaluated languages. However, it may not generalize to all languages or contexts beyond those specifically tested.

What Cannot Be Concluded:
The study cannot conclude that the safety benchmark will universally apply to all LLMs or that improvements in interpretability will directly translate to safety in all contexts. Additionally, the long-term effects beyond the six-month evaluation period are not assessed.
methodology: This study will employ a three-arm design, including a target intervention group utilizing a comprehensive safety benchmark, an active control group with standard prompting strategies, and a usual-care group with no intervention. Participants will consist of diverse large language models (LLMs) evaluated in both Chinese and Spanish contexts. The primary operationalized variables include the rate of unsafe responses (dependent variable), the interpretability of internal representations (mediator), and cultural context adaptability (moderator). Evaluation metrics will include frequency counts of unsafe outputs and interpretability scores derived from established frameworks. Statistical reasoning will involve comparative analyses using ANOVA to assess differences between groups, while controlling for confounding variables such as LLM architecture and language processing capabilities. The study will ensure reproducibility through detailed documentation of methodologies and data sources, focusing on a six-month evaluation period to capture longitudinal effects.

proposal: This research proposal aims to develop interpretable internal representations for enhanced safety and controllability in large language models (LLMs) within multilingual contexts, specifically focusing on non-English languages such as Chinese and Spanish. Existing literature highlights significant safety gaps in LLMs, particularly in multilingual settings, necessitating comprehensive benchmarks to assess safety across diverse applications. The proposed study seeks to empirically evaluate a comprehensive safety benchmark addressing 14 safety issues, utilizing a three-arm design with a target intervention group implementing the benchmark, an active control group with standard prompting strategies, and a usual-care group with no intervention. The independent variable is the safety benchmark, which is expected to enhance the interpretability of internal representations (mediator), thereby reducing the rate of unsafe responses (dependent variable). The hypothesis posits that the implementation of the safety benchmark will significantly reduce unsafe response rates, with improved interpretability mediating this relationship. Operationalization includes measuring unsafe response rates through frequency counts of harmful outputs, interpretability scores using established frameworks, and cultural context adaptability through expert evaluations. The study will employ ANOVA for comparative analyses while controlling for confounding variables such as LLM architecture and language processing capabilities. This research contributes to the field by introducing a novel theoretical framework linking interpretability and safety, employing a rigorous methodological design that addresses critical gaps in multilingual AI deployment, and yielding actionable insights for reliable AI systems. Key limitations include potential variability in LLM architectures, the generalizability of findings beyond the studied languages, and the risk of misinterpreting negative results as ineffective benchmarks.
